Three other price shapes exist alongside monthly retainers: one-time audits ($500 to $5,000), hourly SEO consulting (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-consulting/) ($100 to $300 per hour) and project pricing for a migration or a site rebuild ($3,000 to $30,000). Most businesses end up on a monthly plan, because SEO is ongoing work and the results compound.

### What drives the price

The price of SEO is mostly the price of skilled hours. What changes the number of hours is:

- **Competition.** Ranking a locksmith in a town of 40,000 takes a fraction of the work of ranking a personal injury firm in Los Angeles. Competitive markets need more content, more links and more time.
- **Scope.** One location and five services is a small program. Twelve locations, a product catalog or multiple countries multiplies the pages that need work.
- **Starting point.** A site with technical problems, thin pages or a penalty history needs cleanup before growth work can begin. The SEO audit (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-audit/) is where that gets priced.
- **Goals and speed.** Wanting to lead the market in six months costs more than wanting steady growth over two years, because the work gets front-loaded.
- **Who does the work.** Freelancers, small agencies, large agencies and in-house hires all carry different overheads, and the quality range inside each group is wide.

### What each price level typically includes

| Level | Typical monthly fee | What you usually get | Who it fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starter local | $500 to $1,500 | Google Business Profile management, citation cleanup, a few optimized pages, basic reporting | Single-location service businesses in low to medium competition |
| Growth | $1,500 to $5,000 | Everything in starter plus a content program, link building, technical fixes, multi-location support, a dedicated strategist | Multi-location businesses, regional brands, small online stores, early-stage SaaS |
| Scale | $5,000 to $20,000+ | A full team: strategy, technical, content, digital PR, analytics, often weekly contact | National brands, large e-commerce, funded SaaS, enterprise sites |

RankEmpire's plans sit in the first two rows. Local plans start at $599 a month for one location, Growth and Empire plans scale with tracked keywords, pages per month and link building, and every plan includes the audit, the 90-day roadmap, a named strategist and monthly reporting. Plans are month to month after a three-month onboarding period. The full breakdown is on the pricing page (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/), with separate packages for local SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/local-seo/), e-commerce SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/ecommerce-seo/) and SaaS SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/saas-seo/).

### Why cheap SEO usually costs more

Plans under $500 a month exist, and some are honest about being limited. The problem is the ones that are not. At that price the work has to be automated or outsourced at very low rates, which in practice means spun content, directory spam, purchased links and reports that count things that do not matter. The cleanup afterward, which we are asked to do often, costs more than a proper program would have.

A useful rule: if a quote promises specific rankings, guaranteed first-page results, hundreds of links a month or results in 30 days, the price is irrelevant because the method is going to hurt you. We wrote about the common failure patterns in why most SEO campaigns fail (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/why-most-seo-campaigns-fail/).

### How to compare SEO quotes

Ask every agency the same seven questions and compare the answers rather than the prices:

1. **What exactly is delivered each month?** Pages, content pieces, links, technical tickets, profile updates. Vague "optimization" is not a deliverable.
2. **Who does the work and who do I talk to?** A named strategist who does the work beats an account manager relaying messages.
3. **How do you earn links?** Outreach, PR and content are good answers. Networks, packages and "our partner sites" are not.
4. **What does the first 90 days look like?** A credible agency can describe the sequence: audit, fixes, foundations, then growth. See our 90-day local SEO roadmap (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/local-seo-90-day-roadmap/) for an example.
5. **How do you report?** Rankings and traffic are fine, but calls, leads and revenue from organic should be in the report.
6. **What is the contract?** Month to month after onboarding is fair. Twelve-month lock-ins with no exit protect the agency, not you.
7. **Can I see real results?** Screenshots of Search Console from real clients, with permission, as on our case studies page (https://www.rankempire.us/case-studies/), rather than mockups.

### Is SEO worth the cost for your business?

Run the arithmetic before you sign anything. You need three numbers: the value of a customer, your close rate from leads, and a realistic estimate of extra leads from search.

Take a plumbing company where an average job is worth $450, one in three leads becomes a job, and a solid local program could add 25 leads a month within six months. That is about 8 extra jobs, or $3,600 a month, against a $1,200 plan. The return is clearly positive, and it grows, because rankings compound while the fee stays flat.

Now take a hobby store with a $30 average order and no online sales. Even a strong program might not pay back. SEO is not the right channel for every business, and an honest agency will tell you that in the first call.

The time horizon matters too. SEO rarely pays back inside the first three months, because the early work is foundations. The verified reports on our results page show the same curve on every campaign: impressions move first, then positions, then clicks and leads, usually bending between months three and six.

### SEO cost by business type

- **Local service businesses** (contractors, clinics, salons): $600 to $2,500 a month. The map pack decides most leads, so the profile, reviews and area pages are the bulk of the work. See the industry playbooks, for example SEO for HVAC companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-hvac/) or SEO for dentists (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-dentists/).
- **Multi-location businesses:** $2,000 to $8,000 a month, scaling with locations, since each needs its own profile, page and review flow.
- **E-commerce stores:** $2,000 to $15,000 a month depending on catalog size and competition. Category pages, technical control of faceted navigation and content drive the cost. See e-commerce SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/ecommerce-seo/).
- **SaaS and B2B:** $3,000 to $15,000 a month. Fewer, higher-value keywords, comparison and integration pages, and attribution to pipeline. See SaaS SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/saas-seo/).
- **Luxury, travel and event businesses** (charters, limousines, exotic rentals, venues): $1,500 to $6,000 a month, because fewer searches carry much higher values and route, fleet and venue pages do most of the work. See SEO for private jet charter companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-private-jet-charter/), yacht charter companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-yacht-charter/) and wedding venues and event companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-wedding-venues/).
- **National and enterprise brands:** $8,000 to $30,000+ a month, with dedicated teams and governance. See enterprise SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/enterprise-seo/).

For what the monthly fee actually pays for, see what an SEO company does (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/what-does-an-seo-company-do/).

### One-time costs you might also see

- **SEO audit:** $500 to $5,000 depending on site size. RankEmpire's initial audit is free and delivered within two business days, because it becomes the roadmap if you go ahead.
- **Website migration or redesign support:** $3,000 to $30,000, driven by URL count and complexity. Skipping this is the most common cause of traffic collapse after a redesign.
- **Content production:** $150 to $1,500 per piece depending on depth and expertise, if bought separately from a retainer.
- **Link building campaigns:** $200 to $1,000 per earned editorial link when priced individually. Be suspicious of anything cheaper.

### FAQ

#### How much does SEO cost per month for a small business?

Most small businesses pay between $500 and $2,500 a month. Single-location local service businesses are at the lower end; businesses in competitive metros or with several locations are at the upper end. RankEmpire's local plans start at $599 a month; see SEO services for small business (https://www.rankempire.us/small-business-seo/).

#### Is it cheaper to do SEO yourself?

In cash, yes. In time, usually not. A disciplined owner can handle the basics in about five hours a week using guides like our local SEO checklist (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/local-seo-checklist/) and the free tools on this site. Agencies make sense when that time is worth more spent on the business, or when the market is competitive enough to need specialist work.

#### Why do agencies not publish prices?

Because scope varies, and because some prefer to anchor to your budget. We publish ours because a clear price is easier to compare and keeps the conversation about the work rather than the negotiation.

#### How long do I have to commit?

Avoid long lock-ins. A three-month onboarding period is reasonable because the early work is front-loaded; after that, month to month with 30 days notice is fair. That is how RankEmpire plans work.

#### Does a higher price mean better results?

Not by itself. Price reflects hours and overhead. What predicts results is the method, the people doing the work and the fit between the plan and your market. Use the seven questions above to compare, not the fee, and our longer guide on how to choose an SEO company (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/how-to-choose-an-seo-company/) for the full checklist and red flags.

#### What results should I expect for the money?

Early movement on branded and low-competition terms within four to eight weeks, meaningful ranking gains for core terms in four to six months, and lead growth that compounds from there. Any agency promising specific positions is guessing or cheating.

#### Why is SEO so expensive?

Good SEO is skilled labor spread over months: technical fixes, content written by people who know the subject, reviews and links that have to be earned, and reporting. Most of the fee pays for those hours. Cheap plans usually cut the parts that move rankings, such as content and earned links, which is why they often produce reports but few leads.

#### How much does an SEO audit cost?

A standalone SEO audit commonly costs from about $500 for a small site to $5,000 or more for a large site with complex technical issues. RankEmpire's SEO audit (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-audit/) is free and delivered within two business days.

#### How much does local SEO cost?

Local SEO for a single-location business usually costs about $500 to $1,500 a month, depending on how competitive the city and the service are. Multi-location businesses pay more because each location needs its own profile and pages. RankEmpire's local SEO packages (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/local-seo/) start at $599 a month.

#### How much should SEO cost for a small business?

Enough to pay for real work each month: technical fixes, content and earned links or local signals. For most small businesses that is $500 to $2,500 a month. Plans far below that range usually skip the work that moves rankings.


## Google Business Profile Optimization Checklist: Every Item, in Order
URL: https://www.rankempire.us/blog/google-business-profile-optimization-checklist/
Updated: 2026-11-17

Your Google Business Profile is the most important page you do not host. For most local businesses it produces more calls than the website does, and it is the single biggest factor in whether you appear in the map pack. Most profiles we audit are about a third complete. This checklist is the full list, in the order we work through it for clients, with the reason behind each item so you can prioritize. It is the same process behind our Google Business Profile SEO service (https://www.rankempire.us/google-business-profile-seo/).

### Before you start: ownership and verification

- Confirm you own the profile. Search your business name in Google Maps, click the listing and check for "You manage this Business Profile". If an old employee or agency owns it, request access through the listing before doing anything else.
- Verify it. Unverified profiles have limited features and lower trust. Video verification is the most common method now; have your signage, vehicle and a workspace ready to show.
- Remove duplicates. Search for your phone number and address in Maps. Duplicate listings split reviews and confuse Google. Mark duplicates as "permanently closed" or request a merge through support.
- Check for suspensions. A suspended profile shows a notice in the dashboard. Fix the cause (usually a name, address or category violation) before appealing.

### Business information

- **Business name.** Use your real-world name exactly, with no added keywords or city names. "Joe's Plumbing" is correct; "Joe's Plumbing Houston Emergency Plumber" gets suspended.
- **Primary category.** This is the strongest relevance signal on the profile. Pick the most specific category that describes your main revenue service. "Emergency plumber" or "Plumber", not "Contractor". Check what the top three competitors in the map pack use.
- **Secondary categories.** Add every category that genuinely describes a service you sell. Do not add categories for services you do not offer.
- **Address or service area.** Storefronts show the address. Service area businesses (plumbers, electricians (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-electricians/), cleaners, movers) hide the address and set the cities and zip codes they actually serve. Keep the service area realistic; a 200-mile radius from one van reduces trust.
- **Phone number.** Use a local number as the primary. If you use call tracking, set the tracking number as primary and add your real number as an additional number, so your name, address and phone stay consistent across the web.
- **Website link.** Point it at the most relevant page, which is usually the homepage for single-service businesses and the location page for multi-location businesses.
- **Hours.** Set regular hours and keep them accurate, add special hours for holidays, and set "more hours" (drive-through, pickup, senior hours) where they apply. Wrong hours generate negative reviews.
- **Opening date.** Add it; longevity is a trust signal and it is a required field for some features.

### Services, products and attributes

- **Services.** Add every service with a description of one to two sentences and, where you can, a price or price range. Services feed relevance for searches like "water heater replacement near me" directly. Use Google's suggested services for your category first, then add custom ones.
- **Products.** Retailers and restaurants should add products with photos and prices. Service businesses can use the product section for packages ("Spring HVAC tune-up, $129"). Rental, charter and venue businesses should list each vehicle, yacht or space as a product with a starting price, as we recommend for limousine companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-limousine-companies/), exotic car rentals (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-exotic-car-rental/) and wedding venues (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-wedding-venues/).
- **Attributes.** Fill every attribute that applies: accessibility, payment types, amenities, "women-owned", "veteran-owned", "online appointments" and so on. Attributes appear as filters and as badges in results.
- **Business description.** Up to 750 characters. Lead with what you do and where, in plain language, then what makes you different. Do not stuff keywords; it does not help ranking and it reads badly.

### Photos and video

- Upload at least 20 real photos to start: exterior from the street, interior, team, vehicles, equipment and completed work. Profiles with more photos get more direction requests and calls.
- Add five or more new photos every month. Recency matters.
- Name files descriptively before uploading ("tankless-water-heater-install-katy-tx.jpg") and shoot in good light. Skip stock photos; customers and Google both notice.
- Add a logo and a cover photo that shows the business, not a graphic.
- Add short videos (under 30 seconds) of the team at work. They stand out in the photo carousel.

### Reviews

- Set up a short review link (from the "Ask for reviews" button in the dashboard) and put it everywhere: text message after the job, invoice email, a QR code on a card.
- Ask every customer at the moment of satisfaction. A system that produces four to eight reviews a month beats a one-time push.
- Reply to every review within two days. Thank positive reviewers by name and mention the service. For negative reviews, stay calm, state the facts briefly and take it offline. Future customers read your replies more than the review.
- Never incentivize reviews or gate them (only asking happy customers through a filter). Both violate Google's policies and can wipe out your reviews.
- Report fake reviews through the dashboard, with evidence. It takes time, but it works.

### Posts, Q&A and messaging

- **Posts.** Publish one post a week: a completed project, a seasonal tip, an offer or an event. Posts keep the profile active and give you a place to put calls to action.
- **Q&A.** Anyone can ask and answer questions on your profile, so pre-fill it. Post the ten questions customers ask by phone and answer them from your business account. Monitor for new questions weekly.
- **Messaging.** Turn it on only if someone will respond within a few hours. Slow responses get the feature disabled and look bad.
- **Booking.** If you take appointments, connect a booking provider or add your booking link so customers can book from the profile.

### Consistency across the web

Your name, address and phone must match exactly between the profile, your website, Apple Business Connect, Bing Places, Yelp, Facebook and your industry directories. Inconsistency erodes Google's confidence in your details.

- Write down one canonical format for the name, suite number, phone and hours.
- Fix the major platforms first, then industry directories, then data aggregators.
- Add LocalBusiness schema to your website with the same details and validate it with our free schema checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/schema-checker/).

### Multi-location businesses

- One profile per physical location, each with its own phone, hours, photos and reviews.
- A unique location page on the website for each profile, linked from the profile's website field, with real local detail rather than city-swapped text.
- Use the dashboard's location groups so staff can manage profiles without owner access.
- Keep categories consistent across locations unless the services genuinely differ.

### Track what matters

The profile's own insights show how people found you (discovery versus direct), what they did (calls, direction requests, website clicks) and which searches triggered the listing. Watch three things monthly:

- Calls and direction requests, which are the leads the profile produces.
- The search terms that show your profile. New terms mean growing relevance.
- Your map pack position across your service area, measured on a rank grid rather than from your office, as explained in our 90-day local SEO roadmap (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/local-seo-90-day-roadmap/).

### The checklist in order

1. Claim, verify and clean up duplicates.
2. Set the real name, the most specific primary category and accurate address or service area.
3. Complete services with descriptions, products, attributes and the description.
4. Upload 20 photos and keep adding monthly.
5. Build the review system and reply to everything.
6. Post weekly, pre-fill Q&A, enable messaging only if you can answer.
7. Make name, address and phone identical everywhere, with schema on the site.
8. Track calls, searches and grid position monthly.

Most of this is a one-time setup of a few hours, then an hour a week. If you would rather hand it off, profile management is included in every RankEmpire local SEO plan (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/local-seo/), and a free audit (https://www.rankempire.us/contact-us/) will show you which items your profile is missing today.


### Sources

- Google Business Profile Help: Tips to improve your local ranking on Google (https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en)

### FAQ

#### How long does it take for Google Business Profile changes to affect rankings?

Category and service changes usually show within a few days to two weeks. Reviews, photos and posts compound over months. Profiles that were barely filled in often see map pack movement within the first month of a complete setup.

#### Can I add keywords to my business name?

No. Google's guidelines require the real-world name, and keyword-stuffed names are the most common reason for suspensions. Put the keywords in categories, services and the description instead.

#### How many reviews do I need to rank in the map pack?

Enough to be competitive with the businesses currently showing for your searches, and a steady flow afterward. For most single-location service businesses that is four to eight new reviews a month, every month.

#### Do Google posts help ranking?

Marginally on their own, but active profiles hold positions better and convert more viewers, and posts are a free place to promote offers. One post a week is the right cadence.

#### Should a service area business show its address?

Only if customers visit the location. If they do not, hide the address and set the service area. Showing a home address for a service business is against the guidelines and can get the profile suspended.


## AEO vs GEO vs SEO: How to Get Cited in AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Perplexity
URL: https://www.rankempire.us/blog/aeo-vs-geo-vs-seo/
Updated: 2026-11-17

Search is no longer one results page. The same question now gets answered in a Google AI Overview, a ChatGPT reply, a Perplexity answer with footnotes, a voice assistant and, still, ten blue links. Each surface picks its sources a little differently, and three acronyms have grown up around that: SEO, AEO and GEO.

This guide explains what each one actually changes, how AI answers choose what to cite, and the 12 steps we run for clients who want to be the source, not the footnote that never gets clicked. Everything here is what we do inside the AEO (https://www.rankempire.us/aeo/) and GEO (https://www.rankempire.us/geo/) programs at RankEmpire, with the parts that overlap with classic search engine optimization (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-services/) called out, because most of the work is shared.

### The three terms in one table

| | SEO | AEO | GEO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Full name | Search engine optimization | Answer engine optimization | Generative engine optimization |
| Where you show up | Organic results, map pack, image and video results | Featured snippets, People Also Ask, voice answers, AI Overview citations | ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Copilot answers; AI Overviews and AI Mode |
| What gets rewarded | Pages that satisfy a query better than competing pages | Passages that answer one question directly and can be quoted as-is | Sources that are retrievable, trusted and specific enough to be synthesized into an answer |
| Unit of optimization | The page | The passage | The entity and the claim |
| Primary signals | Relevance, links, technical health, experience | Clear question-and-answer structure, schema, concise definitions | Brand mentions, citations across the web, original data, freshness, crawlability for AI bots |
| How you measure it | Rankings, clicks, conversions | Snippet and PAA ownership, zero-click impressions | Share of citations per prompt, referral traffic from AI assistants |

The important point hides in the second row. SEO, AEO and GEO are not three websites or three teams. They are three ways the same page can be consumed. A service page that ranks well, answers its questions in tight passages and is mentioned across the web will perform on all three surfaces. A page that only does one of those will leak demand to a competitor who does all three.

### What search engine optimization still decides

Nothing about AI search makes classic SEO optional, for a plain reason: the AI systems retrieve their candidate sources from a search index first. Google's AI Overviews are built on top of Google's ranking systems. Perplexity and ChatGPT search run live web queries and read the top results before writing. If your page cannot be crawled, is not indexed, or sits on page four, it is rarely in the candidate set at all.

So the foundation is unchanged:

- Technical health: crawlable, indexable, fast, mobile-first. Our technical SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/technical-seo/) work starts every program because it gates everything else.
- Relevance: one page per intent, with a clear job, built from real keyword research (https://www.rankempire.us/keyword-research/) rather than guesses.
- Authority: links and mentions from sites that matter in your market, earned through link building (https://www.rankempire.us/link-building/) and digital PR.
- Experience: pages that people actually use, measured in clicks, calls and conversions.

Our own verified Search Console reports show what this looks like when it works. One education client went from near zero to 42.1K organic clicks and 240K impressions in six months with a 17.6 percent average click-through rate, on nothing more exotic than fixing the foundation, building the right pages and earning links. You can see that report and eight others on the case studies page (https://www.rankempire.us/case-studies/).

### What answer engine optimization adds

Answer engines take a page and extract a passage. The featured snippet at the top of Google, the People Also Ask accordions, voice assistants reading one sentence aloud, and the citations under an AI Overview all work at the passage level. AEO is the discipline of making your best answer easy to lift.

Three habits make the difference:

1. **Lead with the answer.** Put a direct, complete answer in the first sentence or two under each heading, then expand. Search engines quote the first clean definition they find, not the one buried after three paragraphs of context.
2. **Make headings questions people actually ask.** Google's own People Also Ask boxes and your Search Console query report tell you the exact wording. A heading that mirrors the question is far more likely to be matched to it.
3. **Mark it up.** FAQPage, HowTo, Product, Service, Organization and Person schema label what each block is. Validate it with our free schema checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/schema-checker/) rather than assuming it parses.

AEO is also where zero-click search lives. A large share of informational queries now end on the results page. That is not a loss if the snippet carries your brand name and the next step for the customer is to search for you directly, which is exactly what we see in branded query growth for clients who own the top answers in their category.

### What generative engine optimization changes

Generative engines do something different: they synthesize. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google's AI Mode read several sources, combine them and write an original answer with citations. To be cited you need to be retrieved, trusted and specific. That last word matters most. A generic page that says "we offer quality service at competitive prices" gives a language model nothing to use. A page that says "a two-location dental practice should expect 4 to 6 reviews a month per location to keep pace with the map pack in a mid-sized metro" is a claim a model can quote and attribute.

GEO work therefore concentrates on five things:

- **Entity clarity.** The engines need to know who you are. A consistent name, address and description across your site, Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, Crunchbase, industry directories and press, plus Organization and Person schema that point to those profiles, builds the entity graph the models lean on.
- **Original, quotable information.** First-party data, benchmarks, named processes, prices and timelines. Everything we publish in our case studies (https://www.rankempire.us/case-studies/) is real Search Console data for this reason: real numbers get quoted, vague claims do not.
- **Mentions across the web.** Models weigh how often a brand appears alongside a topic in the corpus they were trained on and in the pages they retrieve. Brand mentions on relevant sites, even unlinked, raise the odds of being named. This is a shift from classic link building, where only the link counted.
- **Freshness.** Retrieval-based engines prefer recently updated sources for anything time-sensitive. Dated, maintained pages with visible update timestamps win over stale ones.
- **Access for AI crawlers.** GPTBot, PerplexityBot and ClaudeBot respect robots.txt; if you block them, those assistants cannot read your pages. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode use the normal Googlebot crawl, so blocking the separate Google-Extended token does not remove you from them; it only limits use of your content in Gemini models. Our robots file allows them on purpose, and we check that with the free robots.txt checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/robots-txt-checker/).

### How AI answers actually pick sources

Nobody outside the labs has the full recipe, but the behavior is observable, and after tracking citations across hundreds of prompts for clients the patterns are consistent enough to act on.

:::kt
Top 10|Most AI citations come from pages that already rank on page one for a closely related query
3 to 5|Typical number of sources cited per generative answer, so the bar is higher than ranking tenth
Passage|Engines cite the specific passage that answered the sub-question, not the page as a whole
:::

What we see repeatedly:

- Citations cluster on pages with clear structure: short paragraphs, descriptive H2 and H3 headings, lists and tables that make a fact easy to extract.
- Pages with a named author, an about page and visible credentials get cited more often than anonymous content on the same topic. Experience and trust are evaluated, not assumed.
- Comparison and "best" queries pull from third-party sources far more than from the brands themselves. If you want to be named in "best SEO agency for dentists", you need to be on the lists other sites publish, not only on your own site.
- Local prompts, such as "good HVAC company near Phoenix", lean heavily on Google Business Profile data, reviews and the same signals that drive the map pack. Local SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/local-seo/) and Google Business Profile optimization (https://www.rankempire.us/google-business-profile-seo/) are GEO for local businesses.
- Numbers get quoted. A page with a benchmark, a price range or a timeline is cited where a page of adjectives is skipped.

### What Google says about AEO and GEO

Google's own documentation is useful here, because it removes a lot of myths:

- **No extra technical requirements.** To appear as a link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, a page must be indexed and eligible to show a snippet in normal Search. Google says there are no additional requirements, and that appearing is still not guaranteed.
- **AEO and GEO are SEO.** Google's guide to its generative AI features says these features are built on Search's ranking and quality systems, so the same SEO practices apply, and it advises caution with services sold under new labels.
- **Measured in Search Console.** Traffic from AI Overviews and AI Mode is included in the Search Console Performance report under Web, and Google has started rolling out a separate generative AI performance report to some sites.
- **Controls are the same as for snippets.** robots.txt, nosnippet and max-snippet decide what Google can show, in AI features as in normal results.

For a business, that means AEO and GEO are not a separate program: clear answers, accurate business facts and strong pages that rank are what get used.

### The overlap, and why you should not run three separate programs

If you draw the three disciplines as circles, around 70 percent of the work sits in the overlap. Technical health, clear information architecture, a page per intent, well-structured content, schema, authority and a visible, consistent brand entity serve all three. The remaining 30 percent is surface-specific: snippet formatting for AEO, citation tracking and mention building for GEO, map pack work for local.

That is why we run them as one program with one roadmap rather than selling AEO and GEO as add-ons. The practical sequence is below.

### The 12-step playbook

1. **Audit crawlability and indexation first.** Confirm every important page is indexed, nothing valuable is blocked, and AI crawlers are allowed. Start with a free SEO audit (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-audit/) if you have never had one.
2. **Map every query to one page.** One intent, one page. Merge cannibalizing pages and split overloaded ones.
3. **Rewrite openings to answer first.** The first 40 to 60 words under each heading should answer the heading's question completely.
4. **Turn headings into real questions.** Pull wording from Search Console, People Also Ask and your sales calls.
5. **Add facts a model can quote.** Prices, timelines, benchmarks, named steps, original data. Replace adjectives with specifics.
6. **Add and validate schema.** Organization with sameAs profiles, Person for authors, Service, FAQPage where the FAQ is unique, Article with dates.
7. **Put a real author on everything.** Name, role, photo, bio page, outside profiles. Link author pages from every article.
8. **Build the entity footprint.** Identical business details on Google, Bing, Apple, LinkedIn, Crunchbase and your industry directories.
9. **Earn mentions, not only links.** Guest contributions, podcasts, roundups, expert quotes and listicles in your category. Measure brand mentions alongside backlinks.
10. **Keep pages fresh.** Visible updated dates, a quarterly review of your top 20 pages, and a changelog of what changed.
11. **Track AI visibility.** Run a fixed set of prompts monthly across AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini and log who gets cited. Our monthly reports include share of voice across these engines next to rankings.
12. **Report revenue, not just rankings.** AI referral traffic converts well because the intent is already qualified. Tag it and track it to calls and sales.

### A worked example: one service page, three surfaces

Take a page about emergency plumbing in Houston. For classic search it needs the basics: title, H1, service details, reviews, internal links from the Houston location page and the plumbers industry page (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-plumbers/) (the same pattern works for electricians (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-electricians/)), and a few local citations. For answer engines it needs a short passage that says exactly what a 24-hour callout costs and how fast a plumber arrives, under a heading that asks that question. For generative engines it needs the business to appear on lists of Houston plumbers, a profile with consistent details, reviews that mention emergency work, and a page that was updated this quarter rather than three years ago.

Same page. One roadmap. Three ways of being found.

### How to measure progress

Set a baseline before you change anything, then track monthly:

- Classic: rankings for your 20 primary keywords, organic clicks, calls and leads from organic.
- Answer engines: which snippets and People Also Ask results you own, impressions on queries where you have no clicks (a sign you are the zero-click answer).
- Generative engines: a prompt set of 30 to 50 questions your customers ask, run across the main assistants, scored by whether you are named, cited or linked. Share of voice against three competitors.
- Entity: brand search volume, brand mentions, referring domains.

If the generative numbers lag while classic rankings are strong, the usual causes are missing specifics, no named author, or thin presence on third-party lists. If classic rankings lag, go back to the foundation.

### The next surface: AI agents

Answers are turning into actions. Assistants increasingly compare providers, request quotes and book on a user's behalf, which adds a fourth discipline on top of SEO, AEO and GEO: making your business easy for an agent to verify and transact with. We cover it in depth in what AI agent optimization is (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/ai-agent-optimization/), including a 10-step agent-readiness checklist.


### Sources

- Google Search Central: AI features and your website (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)
- Google Search Central Blog: Top ways to ensure your content performs well in Google's AI experiences on Search (https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2025/05/succeeding-in-ai-search)
- Google Search Central Blog: Introducing Search generative AI performance reports in Search Console (https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports)
- Google Business Profile Help: Tips to improve your local ranking on Google (https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en)

### FAQ

#### Is AEO or GEO replacing SEO?

No. Both depend on the same search indexes and ranking systems to find candidate sources. SEO gets you into the candidate set, AEO makes your passage the one that gets quoted, and GEO makes your brand the one that gets named. Treat them as layers on one program.

#### How long does it take to get cited in AI Overviews or ChatGPT?

For pages that already rank on page one, structural changes often show up in citations within four to eight weeks. For new topics, expect three to six months, the same horizon as classic SEO, because you first need to rank and build the entity signals.

#### Should I block AI crawlers to protect my content?

If you want to be cited, no. Blocking GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot or Google-Extended removes you from those answers. Publishers with content they license may choose to block; service businesses almost always benefit from being included.

#### Does FAQ schema still help?

Google has reduced FAQ rich results for most commercial sites, so do not expect the dropdowns in results. The structure still helps answer and generative engines parse your questions and answers, and it costs nothing when the FAQ is genuinely unique to the page.

#### Can a small local business do GEO?

Yes, and it is often easier than for national brands because the competition in a metro is thinner. A complete Google Business Profile, consistent citations, steady reviews, a page per service with specific details and a few local mentions will get a local business named in AI answers for its category and city.

#### What does RankEmpire include for AEO and GEO?

Every plan includes AI Overview and citation tracking, an entity and schema layer, citation-worthy content and a monthly AI visibility report next to your rankings. See the AEO service page (https://www.rankempire.us/aeo/), the GEO service page (https://www.rankempire.us/geo/) and the SEO packages (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/) for what is included at each level.


## Local SEO for Service Businesses: The 90-Day Roadmap, With Real Search Console Data
URL: https://www.rankempire.us/blog/local-seo-90-day-roadmap/
Updated: 2026-10-28

Most local SEO advice is a list of 40 things to do with no order and no timeline. This is the opposite: the 90-day sequence we run for service businesses, in the order that moves the map pack fastest, with the Search Console numbers from a real home services campaign so you know what "working" looks like at each stage.

It is written for contractors, clinics and any business where the customer searches "near me", looks at the map, reads a few reviews and calls. If that is you, the first 90 days decide whether SEO becomes a lead source or an expense. The plan below is the same one behind our local SEO service (https://www.rankempire.us/local-seo/), and you can run most of it yourself.

### Why 90 days, and what to expect each month

Google's local results are driven by three things the company itself names: relevance, distance and prominence. You cannot change distance, so the work is about relevance (does your profile and site clearly match the search) and prominence (how well known and well reviewed you are). Relevance can be fixed in weeks. Prominence compounds over months. That is why the roadmap front-loads profile and site fixes and back-loads reviews, pages and links.

:::kt
Weeks 1 to 4|Fix what is wrong: profile, site, citations. Movement on branded and low-competition terms
Weeks 5 to 8|Build what is missing: service and area pages, review system. First map pack gains in your core area
Weeks 9 to 13|Earn prominence: links, content, local mentions. Visibility spreads across the service area
:::

Here is what a real campaign produced in its first three months, from a home services company's Search Console account, published with permission.

!Google Search Console performance report for a home services company showing 5.85K clicks and 822K impressions over three months (https://www.rankempire.us/img/r-gsc7.webp "Home services company, three months: 5.85K clicks, 822K impressions, 0.7 percent CTR, 33.4 average position. The low CTR and high impressions are typical early on: the site starts appearing for many searches before it ranks high enough to be clicked. Clicks follow as positions climb.")

Notice the shape. Impressions grow first, then average position improves, then clicks. If you only track clicks in month one you will think nothing is happening. Track impressions and position too.

### Weeks 1 to 2: audit and Google Business Profile

Start with a baseline so you can prove progress later. Record your map pack position for your five most valuable searches from three points in your service area (not just your office), your current review count and rating, and your Search Console clicks and impressions for the last 28 days. Our free keyword rank checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/keyword-rank-checker/) and website SEO checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/website-seo-checker/) cover the basics in a few minutes.

Then fix the profile, because it is the single biggest lever in the map pack:

- **Primary category.** Choose the most specific category that matches your main revenue service. "HVAC contractor" beats "contractor". Add secondary categories for other real services.
- **Services and descriptions.** Add every service you sell with a two-sentence description. These feed relevance directly.
- **Business details.** Hours, phone, website link to the right landing page (not always the homepage), service area set to the cities you actually serve.
- **Photos.** Twenty or more real photos: team, vehicles, completed work, office. Add five more every month. Stock photos do nothing.
- **Attributes and Q&A.** Fill every attribute that applies and pre-answer the ten questions customers ask by phone.
- **Posts.** One post per week from here on: a job you completed, a seasonal tip, an offer.

Finish the two weeks with a technical pass on the website. Confirm the site is indexable, loads in under three seconds on a phone, has one page per core service, and that the name, address and phone number on the site match the profile exactly. Anything broken here caps everything that follows, which is why our programs begin with an SEO audit (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-audit/).

### Weeks 3 to 4: citations and the website foundation

Citations are mentions of your business name, address and phone number on other sites. They are no longer a ranking rocket, but inconsistent ones actively hurt, because Google loses confidence in which details are correct.

- Fix the big four first: Google, Apple Business Connect, Bing Places and Yelp.
- Then the data aggregators and the directories specific to your industry (for example, Houzz for remodelers, Healthgrades for clinics, Avvo for law firms).
- Use one canonical format for the name, suite number, phone and hours everywhere. Write it down and reuse it.

On the website, the foundation work is:

1. A dedicated page for each core service with real detail: process, pricing ranges, timelines, photos, FAQs. Our industry pages, for example SEO for HVAC companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-hvac/) and SEO for plumbers (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-plumbers/), show the page structure we use.
2. A contact page with the full business details, an embedded map and a form that works on phones.
3. Internal links from the homepage to every service page, and from every service page to the contact page and the relevant area page.
4. LocalBusiness schema with the same details as the profile, validated with the schema checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/schema-checker/).

By the end of week four most businesses see their branded searches and a few low-competition service terms move. That is the profile and the site becoming clearly relevant.

### Weeks 5 to 8: service area pages and the review system

#### Service area pages that are not duplicates

If you serve several cities or neighborhoods, each important one deserves a page, but only if the page says something true and specific about that area. Pages that swap the city name and keep everything else are the most common reason local sites get filtered. For each area include: projects completed there, local regulations or permit notes, typical travel time, nearby landmarks you serve, and reviews from customers in that area. Our city pages, such as SEO company in Miami (https://www.rankempire.us/locations/miami/) and SEO company in Chicago (https://www.rankempire.us/locations/chicago/), follow the same rule: every one is written for its market, not generated.

Link each area page from the main service pages and from a "service areas" section on the homepage. Keep the count honest. Five strong area pages beat thirty thin ones.

#### A review system you can keep running

Reviews are the prominence signal you control most directly, and they influence the click as much as the ranking. Build a system in week five and never stop:

- Ask at the moment of satisfaction, in person or by text, with a direct link to the review form.
- Ask every customer, not just the happy-looking ones. Volume and recency both matter.
- Reply to every review within two days. Replies to negative reviews are read by future customers more than the reviews themselves.
- Never incentivize or gate reviews. It breaks the platform rules and the penalty is losing them all.

A realistic target for a single-location service business is four to eight new Google reviews per month. Where a competitor has 300 reviews and you have 30, this is also the gap that decides the map pack, and it only closes with a system.

### Weeks 9 to 13: links, content and local prominence

With relevance fixed, the last month is about becoming known in your market. This is the part most local businesses skip, and it is where the campaign above went from impressions to clicks.

- **Local links.** Sponsor a youth team, join the chamber of commerce, partner with complementary businesses, get listed on supplier and manufacturer sites, pitch a local news story. Each is a link from a site that is clearly local, which is the strongest prominence signal most competitors lack. See how we approach this in link building (https://www.rankempire.us/link-building/).
- **Helpful content for your area.** Cost guides, seasonal checklists, "what to do when" pages. A plumber's "what to do when a pipe bursts" page earns links and brings in the customer who needs a plumber tonight.
- **Google Business Profile posts and photos** continue weekly. Profiles with recent activity hold positions better than dormant ones.
- **Expand service pages** with FAQs pulled from Search Console queries and People Also Ask, which also feeds the answer engine (https://www.rankempire.us/aeo/) side of search.

### Tracking the right way: the rank grid

Map rankings change by where the searcher is standing. Checking from your office tells you almost nothing about the customer eight miles away. Use a grid-based tracker: a set of points across your service area, each checked for your main keywords, colored by position. The home page of this site shows what one looks like. Before the roadmap, most businesses are green near the office and red everywhere else. The goal of the 90 days is to turn the ring around your office green, then push outward.

Report monthly on five numbers: points in the top three on the grid, average grid position, Google Business Profile calls and direction requests, organic clicks, and leads from organic. The last one is the only one your accountant cares about.

### Common mistakes that stall local campaigns

1. **Starting with content before the profile and site are fixed.** Articles on a site with a half-empty profile and mismatched citations do not rank.
2. **Keyword stuffing the business name.** "Joe's Plumbing Houston Emergency Plumber 24/7" gets suspended. Use your real name.
3. **One page listing ten services.** It ranks for none of them. One service, one page.
4. **Fake area pages.** City-swapped pages get filtered and drag the rest of the site down with them.
5. **Stopping reviews after the first push.** Recency matters. A burst of reviews in March followed by silence looks worse by August than a steady four a month.
6. **Quitting in month three.** The curve bends between months three and six, as the Search Console report above shows. Most failed campaigns were stopped just before that.

### What this costs and when to get help

Everything above can be done in-house by a disciplined owner or office manager with about five hours a week, and SEO consulting (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-consulting/) can supply the plan and reviews if you want a second pair of eyes. Where businesses bring us in is when they lack that time, serve multiple locations, or are in a market where the competitors already have a hundred reviews and a page for every suburb. Our local SEO packages (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/local-seo/) start with a single-location plan that covers the profile, citations, review system, area pages and the rank grid report, month to month after onboarding. If you want to know where you stand first, request a free audit (https://www.rankempire.us/contact-us/) and we will send the baseline and the 90-day plan for your business.

### Getting your business ready for AI agents

The same foundations, consistent listings, published prices and a simple booking path, are what AI assistants need when they compare and book local services for users. If you are finishing this roadmap, the next step is our AI agent optimization checklist (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/ai-agent-optimization/).

### FAQ

#### How long does local SEO take to work?

Profile and relevance fixes often show movement within two to four weeks on branded and low-competition searches. Competitive map pack terms usually take three to six months, because prominence signals like reviews and local links compound over time.

#### Do I need a separate page for every city I serve?

Only for the areas that matter commercially and only if you can write something true and specific about each one. A handful of detailed area pages outperform dozens of city-swapped duplicates, which Google filters.

#### How many Google reviews do I need?

Enough to match or beat the businesses currently in the map pack for your searches, and a steady flow afterward. For most single-location service businesses that means four to eight new reviews a month, every month.

#### Should I use a tracking number on my Google Business Profile?

Yes, if you set the tracking number as the primary number and list your real number as an additional number, so the name, address and phone details stay consistent across the web. Call tracking is how you prove the profile is producing leads.

#### What is a local rank grid?

A map of your service area divided into points, each showing where you rank for a keyword when the search happens from that spot. It replaces the misleading single check from your office with a true picture of visibility across the whole area.

#### Can local SEO help if I do not have a storefront?

Yes. Service area businesses can hide their address and set the areas they serve. The roadmap is the same, with more weight on area pages, reviews that mention locations, and local links, since there is no storefront prominence to lean on.


## Why Most SEO Campaigns Fail in the First 6 Months
URL: https://www.rankempire.us/blog/why-most-seo-campaigns-fail/
Updated: 2026-10-28

Most SEO campaigns do not fail because SEO stopped working. They fail because the work is done in the wrong order, measured with the wrong numbers, or abandoned right before it starts paying off. After running programs for local businesses, online stores and SaaS companies, the same seven mistakes account for almost every stalled campaign we are asked to rescue. Here they are, with what to do instead.

### 1. Content before foundation

Publishing articles on a site that Google struggles to crawl is like stocking shelves in a store with a locked front door. If key pages are blocked, slow, duplicated or buried six clicks deep, new content will not perform, no matter how good it is.

The fix is sequencing. Crawlability, indexation, site speed and internal linking come first, which is why every RankEmpire program opens with a technical SEO audit (https://www.rankempire.us/technical-seo/). Only once the foundation is sound does content get the green light. If you want a quick sanity check before you spend on writing, our free website SEO checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/website-seo-checker/) and sitemap checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/sitemap-checker/) catch the most common blockers in minutes.

### 2. Targeting keywords without intent

A keyword with high volume is useless if the people searching it do not want what you sell. Every target should be checked against the current results page. If Google shows guides and comparison articles and you have a sales page, you are fighting the algorithm instead of working with it. If Google shows a map pack and you have a blog post, the same.

Good keyword research (https://www.rankempire.us/keyword-research/) sorts every term by what the searcher wants (to learn, to compare, to buy, to find a local provider) and matches a page type to each. The campaigns that work target fewer keywords with the right page for each, not hundreds with the wrong one.

### 3. One page trying to rank for everything

Service pages that list ten services rarely rank for any of them. Each meaningful service, location and audience deserves its own page with a clear job. This is also how you avoid keyword cannibalization, where several of your own pages compete for the same search and Google picks neither.

The test is simple: for each important search, can you name the one page on your site that should rank for it? If the answer is "the homepage" for everything, or two pages for the same term, the architecture is the problem. Our industry pages, for example SEO for dentists (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-dentists/) and SEO for roofing companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-roofing/), exist precisely because one generic "SEO services" page cannot serve forty different markets.

### 4. Thin or templated pages at scale

The opposite failure is just as common: generating hundreds of near-identical pages for every city and service combination. Google's systems are good at spotting pages whose only difference is a swapped noun, and the usual outcome is "crawled, currently not indexed" for the lot, which then drags down the pages that deserved to rank.

Scale only where you can be specific. A page for a city should contain things true only of that city. A page for a service should answer the questions only that service raises. Where you cannot say anything unique, do not build the page.

### 5. Measuring the wrong thing

Rankings and traffic are leading indicators, not outcomes. Plenty of campaigns report a rising graph of "keywords in the top 100" while the phone stays silent. Track calls, form submissions, booked appointments and revenue from organic search. When the report connects to money, decisions get easier, and the strategy corrects itself, because you stop chasing terms that do not convert.

This is also why every result we publish is a real Search Console report rather than a rank tracker screenshot. Clicks, impressions and click-through rate from Google's own data, as shown on our case studies page (https://www.rankempire.us/case-studies/), are harder to game and closer to revenue than a position number.

### 6. Buying authority instead of earning it

Link schemes, private blog networks and bulk directory submissions still get sold, and they still get sites filtered or penalized. Worse, the damage often appears months later, when it is hard to connect cause and effect.

Authority that lasts comes from the boring sources: real mentions in your industry, local organizations, suppliers and partners, guest contributions, original data that other sites cite, and digital PR. Our link building (https://www.rankempire.us/link-building/) work is slower than buying a package of 500 links, and it is also the only kind that is still working in year three.

### 7. Quitting at month four

SEO compounds. Months one to three are mostly fixes and foundations. Months four to six bring the first meaningful movement. The real returns usually show after that. Most campaigns that fail are stopped just before the curve bends.

The verified reports on our results page show the same shape every time: impressions rise first, then positions, then clicks and leads. One education client's report runs from near zero to 42.1K clicks over six months, and the first two months of that chart are nearly flat. Judge a campaign on whether the leading indicators are moving in order, not on whether the phone rang in month two.

To check where your own campaign stands, see how to tell if your SEO is working (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/how-to-tell-if-seo-is-working/).

### The sequence that works

Put the seven mistakes in reverse and you get the plan:

1. **Audit first.** Technical health, indexation, current rankings, competitors, conversion tracking. Our SEO audit (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-audit/) produces a prioritized 90-day plan from this.
2. **Fix the foundation.** Crawl, index, speed, structure, internal links.
3. **Map intent to pages.** One intent, one page. Merge, split and build as needed.
4. **Build pages with one clear job**, specific to their service, audience or location.
5. **Earn real authority** through mentions, partnerships, PR and content worth citing.
6. **Measure revenue**, with calls and forms tracked back to organic search.
7. **Keep going past month four**, reviewing the roadmap monthly and reallocating effort to what is moving.

It is not glamorous, but it is how rankings become an asset instead of an expense. If your current campaign is missing any of the first three steps, that is the place to start. Before you hire anyone, read how to choose an SEO company (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/how-to-choose-an-seo-company/) for the twelve questions that expose these mistakes in a proposal. If you would like a second opinion on a stalled program, request a free audit (https://www.rankempire.us/contact-us/) and we will tell you plainly where it went off sequence.

### FAQ

#### How long should I give an SEO campaign before judging it?

Six months, provided the leading indicators (indexed pages, impressions, average position) are moving in the right order from month two. If nothing has moved by month four, including impressions, the sequencing or the foundation is wrong.

#### Is it the agency's fault or the website's?

Usually both are involved. A good agency audits the site first and tells you what has to change before content and links can work. If a campaign started with articles or links and skipped the audit, the order was wrong regardless of who did the work.

#### Can a failed campaign be rescued?

Almost always. The typical rescue is an audit (a short SEO consulting (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-consulting/) engagement works well if your team will do the fixes), a cleanup of thin or duplicated pages, a rebuild of the page-per-intent structure, conversion tracking, and then a return to earning authority. Progress tends to be faster than a fresh start because some authority already exists.

#### What is a realistic SEO budget for a small business?

It depends on the market, but our SEO packages (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/) start at single-location local plans and scale to multi-location and national programs. The right budget is the one that funds the full sequence above rather than a piece of it.


## The Local SEO Checklist for Service Businesses
URL: https://www.rankempire.us/blog/local-seo-checklist/
Updated: 2026-11-17

The map pack is where local customers decide who to call. This checklist covers the work that moves map rankings, in the order we do it for clients, with the numbers to track each month so you know it is working. If you want the week-by-week version with real Search Console data, read the 90-day local SEO roadmap (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/local-seo-90-day-roadmap/) after this.

### Google Business Profile

Your profile is the single biggest lever in local search. Most businesses fill in a third of it.

- Choose the most specific primary category that matches your main revenue service, then add secondary categories for the other services you genuinely offer.
- Add every service you offer with a short, specific description. These feed relevance directly.
- Set the website link to the most relevant landing page, not always the homepage.
- Set your service area to the cities and neighborhoods you actually serve.
- Upload real photos of your team, vehicles, location and work. Twenty to start, five more every month. Stock photos do nothing.
- Post at least weekly: completed jobs, seasonal tips, offers and updates.
- Fill every attribute that applies (accessibility, payment types, amenities).
- Answer common questions in the Q&A section before customers ask them.
- Turn on messaging only if someone will answer within a few hours.

Deep profile work, including category strategy and ongoing posts, is what our Google Business Profile SEO (https://www.rankempire.us/google-business-profile-seo/) service covers.

### Consistency across the web

Your business name, address and phone number should match exactly across your website, Google, Apple Business Connect, Bing Places, Yelp, Facebook and the directories specific to your industry. Inconsistent listings confuse both search engines and customers, and they quietly cap your map rankings.

- Write down one canonical format for the name, suite, phone and hours, and reuse it everywhere.
- Fix the big four first: Google, Apple, Bing, Yelp. Then aggregators and industry directories.
- Remove or correct old listings from previous addresses or phone numbers.
- Add LocalBusiness schema to your site with the same details, and validate it with the free schema checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/schema-checker/).

### Reviews

Reviews drive the ranking and the click. The business with 300 recent reviews at 4.8 will usually beat the one with 30 at 5.0, so volume and recency matter as much as the score.

- Ask every happy customer, with a direct link, at the moment of satisfaction.
- Build it into the process: a text after the job, a card with a QR code, a line in the invoice email.
- Respond to every review within a few days, positive or negative. Future customers read the replies.
- Never buy reviews or offer incentives that break platform rules. The penalty is losing all of them.
- Target four to eight new Google reviews a month per location and keep it steady.

### Location and service pages

Create a page for each core service and each important area you serve. Include real details: projects completed nearby, local regulations, travel times, photos and reviews from that area. Avoid copying the same text with the city name swapped, which is the most common reason local pages get filtered out of the index.

- One service, one page. Pages listing ten services rank for none.
- Area pages only where you can say something true and specific about the area.
- Link every service page to the contact page and to the relevant area pages, and link the homepage to all of them.
- Add FAQs pulled from the questions customers actually ask by phone. These also feed answer engines (https://www.rankempire.us/aeo/).

Our industry playbooks show the page structure for specific markets, for example SEO for plumbers (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-plumbers/), SEO for electricians (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-electricians/), SEO for dentists (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-dentists/) and SEO for landscaping companies (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-for-landscaping/).

### Technical basics

A slow or broken site caps everything above. The checks that matter for a local business are short:

- The site loads in under three seconds on a phone.
- Every important page is indexed and linked from the navigation or the homepage.
- Name, address, phone and hours on the site match the profile exactly.
- The contact form works on a phone and sends to someone who answers.
- There is one version of the site (www or non-www, https) and the rest redirect to it.

Run the free website SEO checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/website-seo-checker/) for a quick pass, or read technical SEO basics (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/technical-seo-basics/) for the plain-English version of each check.

### Local links

Sponsor local teams and events, join your chamber of commerce, partner with complementary businesses, get listed on supplier and manufacturer locator pages, and pitch local news stories. Local links are a strong prominence signal that most competitors never build.

- Aim for two to four genuinely local links a month.
- Prioritize sites that are clearly about your city or your industry over generic directories.
- Avoid paid link packages. They are the fastest way to lose what you have built.

### Track the right way

Map rankings change by location. Checking from your office tells you almost nothing about the customer across town. Use a grid-based rank tracker to see visibility across your whole service area, then report monthly on:

- Points in the top three on the rank grid, and average grid position.
- Google Business Profile calls, direction requests and website clicks.
- Organic clicks and impressions from Search Console.
- Leads and revenue from organic search.

Expect impressions to move first, then positions, then clicks and calls. The verified Search Console reports (https://www.rankempire.us/case-studies/) on our results page show that shape on every campaign.

### The checklist, in order

1. Complete the Google Business Profile.
2. Fix citations on the big four, then industry directories.
3. Build the review system and start asking.
4. Fix the technical basics on the site.
5. Build one page per service and per real service area.
6. Earn two to four local links a month.
7. Track with a rank grid and report on leads.

If you would rather hand this off, our local SEO packages (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-packages/local-seo/) cover every item above, month to month after onboarding. A free audit (https://www.rankempire.us/contact-us/) will tell you which items are already done and which are costing you the map pack.

Running a trade business? Our SEO for contractors guide (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/seo-for-contractors/) applies this checklist to plumbers, electricians, roofers, HVAC companies and other home service contractors.

Need keyword ideas for your trade? Our SEO keywords by industry (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/seo-keywords-by-industry/) guide lists service, urgent, cost, local and question keywords for 15 industries.


### Sources

- Google Business Profile Help: Tips to improve your local ranking on Google (https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en)

### FAQ

#### What matters most for ranking in the Google map pack?

Relevance (a complete profile and site that clearly match the search), distance (which you cannot change) and prominence (reviews, links and mentions). The profile and reviews are the fastest levers; links and mentions compound over months.

#### How often should I post on Google Business Profile?

Weekly is enough to keep the profile active. Posts are a minor ranking factor on their own, but profiles with recent activity hold positions better and convert more viewers into calls.

#### Do citations still matter for local SEO?

Consistent citations matter; volume does not. Fix the major platforms and your industry's directories, make every listing identical, and stop there. Hundreds of low-quality directory listings add nothing.


## Technical SEO Basics Every Business Owner Should Know
URL: https://www.rankempire.us/blog/technical-seo-basics/
Updated: 2026-10-28

Technical SEO sounds intimidating, but the core ideas are simple: Google needs to find your pages, understand them and load them quickly. You do not need to be a developer to check whether that is happening. Here are the seven checks we run first on every new client site, in plain English, with a free tool for each.

### 1. Can Google find your pages?

Every important page should be linked from somewhere on your site and listed in your XML sitemap. Pages nobody links to, called orphan pages, are hard for Google to discover and easy for it to forget. A sitemap is the list of URLs you want indexed; it should contain only pages that return a 200 status and have no canonical pointing elsewhere.

- Check that your sitemap exists (usually at /sitemap.xml) and is referenced in robots.txt.
- Make sure it lists only live, indexable pages, with an accurate last-modified date.
- Submit it in Google Search Console and watch the "Pages" report for anything excluded.

Use our free sitemap checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/sitemap-checker/) to count URLs, spot duplicates and catch format errors.

### 2. Are you blocking anything by accident?

Your robots.txt file tells crawlers what they may visit. One wrong line can block an entire section of the site, or every AI crawler that might have cited you. Common accidents include a leftover "Disallow: /" from a staging site, blocked CSS and JavaScript folders, and blocked image directories.

Test your important URLs, and the user agents that matter (Googlebot, Bingbot, GPTBot, PerplexityBot), with the free robots.txt checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/robots-txt-checker/).

### 3. Is each page unique and indexable?

Duplicate pages split ranking signals. The same product under three URLs, http and https versions, www and non-www, trailing slash and no trailing slash, and tracking parameters all create copies. Use canonical tags to point every duplicate to the main version, and give each page a unique title and description.

- Pick one domain version and redirect the others to it with a 301.
- Add a self-referencing canonical tag on every page.
- Check that no important page carries a "noindex" tag by mistake, a frequent leftover from launches.

Our meta tag checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/meta-tag-checker/) shows the title, description, canonical and robots tags for any page in one view.

### 4. Is the site fast on phones?

Google evaluates the mobile version of your site first, and its Core Web Vitals measure how fast the main content appears (Largest Contentful Paint), how quickly the page responds to taps (Interaction to Next Paint) and whether things jump around while loading (Cumulative Layout Shift). Large images, heavy scripts and slow hosting hurt both rankings and conversions.

The fixes with the biggest payoff, in order:

1. Compress images and serve modern formats (WebP or AVIF), sized for the screen they appear on.
2. Remove scripts you do not need. Every tracking pixel and chat widget costs time.
3. Load fonts from your own domain and limit them to two families.
4. Use a content delivery network and decent hosting. Cheap shared hosting is a common ceiling.
5. Set explicit width and height on images and embeds so the layout does not shift.

Check your real-user scores in the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console, which reflects what visitors actually experience rather than a lab test.

### 5. Does Google understand what you are?

Structured data, or schema markup, labels your business, services, products, reviews, articles and FAQs in a format search engines read directly. It can unlock rich results and it helps answer engines and AI assistants understand who you are and what you offer, which is a growing part of answer engine optimization (https://www.rankempire.us/aeo/).

The minimum for a business site:

- Organization or LocalBusiness, with your name, logo, contact details and links to your social profiles.
- Service for each service page, and Product for products.
- Article with a named author and dates on every blog post.
- BreadcrumbList so Google shows your site structure in results.

Validate yours with our free schema checker (https://www.rankempire.us/seo-tools/schema-checker/), and fix errors before adding more types.

### 6. Is the site structure shallow and linked?

Google and visitors should reach any important page in three clicks or fewer from the homepage. Deep pages get crawled less and rank worse. Internal links also tell Google which pages matter most: the pages you link to from the navigation, the homepage and the body of other pages are the ones that get crawled first and ranked highest.

- Link every service page from the homepage and the main navigation.
- Link related pages to each other in the body text, with descriptive anchor text rather than "click here".
- Keep the navigation focused on the pages that matter rather than listing everything.
- Fix broken links and redirect chains, which waste crawl budget and leak authority.

### 7. Has anything been lost in a migration or redesign?

Traffic drops after a redesign are almost always technical: URLs changed without redirects, pages were dropped, canonical or noindex tags were copied from staging, or the new site is slower. Before any redesign, export every URL that gets traffic from Search Console and map each one to its new address. After launch, crawl the new site and compare.

If the drop has already happened, the recovery is the same list in reverse: restore redirects, remove stray noindex tags, re-submit the sitemap and watch the Pages report recover over a few weeks.

### When to get help

If pages will not index, traffic dropped after a redesign, or your site is slow despite the fixes above, it is time for a professional technical SEO audit (https://www.rankempire.us/technical-seo/). We start every program with one because the foundation decides what every later piece of work can achieve, which is also the first lesson in why most SEO campaigns fail (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/why-most-seo-campaigns-fail/). You can request a free audit (https://www.rankempire.us/contact-us/) and get a prioritized list within two business days.

For a real example of these checks in action, see how we took our own site from 17 to 123 indexed pages (https://www.rankempire.us/blog/how-we-got-our-pages-indexed/), with the Search Console data behind each step.

### FAQ

#### What is the difference between crawling and indexing?

Crawling is Google visiting a page and reading it. Indexing is Google deciding to store it and make it eligible to appear in results. A page can be crawled and still excluded from the index if it is a duplicate, thin, blocked by a noindex tag, or judged not useful enough.

#### How do I know if Google has indexed my page?

Use the URL Inspection tool in Google Search Console. It shows whether the page is indexed, when it was last crawled, the canonical Google chose, and any blocking issues. The Pages report lists every excluded URL with the reason.

#### Does site speed really affect rankings?

Yes, through Core Web Vitals, and it affects conversions even more. The ranking effect is modest between two fast sites but significant when a site fails the thresholds on mobile.

#### How often should I run a technical audit?

A full audit once a year, or after any redesign, platform change or migration. Monthly, check the Pages and Core Web Vitals reports in Search Console for anything new.
